newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS STANDARDS UNDER SCRUTINY.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS STANDARDS UNDER SCRUTINY.

text.p: Outdated, over-rated, parochial and in dire need of fresh impetus? Or still the jewel in the crown of northern hemisphere rugby and the envy of sports marketers everywhere?
For the vast majority of supporters planning to enjoy a few drinks in Edinburgh and Dublin this weekend, those questioning the merits of the Five Nations championship are simply killjoys.

But among the players, coaches and administrators there is a nagging feeling that the latest edition of the tournament, which kicks off on Saturday, represents the last chance for some individuals and perhaps the traditional concept as a whole.

Italy's argument for extending the 'club' to six nations is an overwhelming one in any case, their recent victory over Ireland merely highlighting the modest current form of their so-called superiors.

The Irish have also lost dismally this season to Western Samoa, an injury-hit Australian side proved far too good for all the Celtic nations, France have been beaten twice at home by South Africa and England were lucky not to lose at home to Argentina last month.

In the professional era, with a rising number of big overseas names raising standards at club level in England at least, few can afford to keep under-performing for long if they want to stay household names and be paid accordingly.

Apart from anything else, European players will be anxious to avoid unfavourable comparisons with the southern hemisphere Super 12 tournament which made such a stunning impact last year, while this year's British Lions tour to South Africa is also looming.
Satellite television means the Five Nations can now be monitored live from Calcutta to Christchurch and no-one will be watching more avidly than Springbok coach Andre Markgraaf.
England, who sit out the opening round, are pre-tournament favourites to win the 1997 title and will provide the bulk of what coach Ian McGeechan has indicated will be the biggest-ever Lions squad.

Yet there are still political rumblings on the domestic scene, the Rugby Football Union have had to give beleaguered coach Jack Rowell a "vote of confidence" and England must travel to both Lansdowne Road and Cardiff Arms Park, grounds where they have misfired in the past.

Wales are embarking on approximately their 10th new dawn since their halcyon days of the 1970s and must hope their recalled rugby league men such as Scott Quinnell and Scott Gibbs provide the extra attacking muscle they need.

Ireland are in apparent disarray after dismissing New Zealander Murray Kidd as coach last week, while nothing Scotland have done at either international or provincial level this season suggests they are set to improve on last year's second place.

That leaves the French with an excellent chance to collect their first title for four years, assuming they can overcome the absence of injured captain Philippe Saint-Andre and not allow Ireland to steal their first win in the fixture for 14 years on the opening day.

Last year, England won the title on points difference despite scoring just three tries, the lowest ever recorded by the winners, and their impoverished strike-rate said a lot about the overall standard.

Australia, New Zealand and South Africa all possess dazzling strike runners at full-back in Matt Burke, Christian Cullen and Andre Joubert respectively but it is now almost five years since a Five Nations try was scored by an English, Welsh or Irish number 15.

Such damning statistics cannot be tolerated under the new laws and the most telling pre-tournament words have come from New Zealand coach John Hart who believes England are "obsessed by height and weight rather than speed and handling".

"I'm sure coaches and players will respond to the (law) changes and produce a faster, more attacking game," Hart added. "Strong northern hemisphere teams are essential to produce a competitive, global game needed to attract media, television and sponsors."
